Knowable Magazine Whether it’s gushing from a bumped nose or pooling atop a pricked finger, our blood is some hue of red. But red-bloodedness isn’t universal in the animal kingdom. In some creatures, the vital fluid is purple; in others it’s yellow, green or even white. What imparts these different colors to the liquid of life? Bizarre blues and purples The rich red of vertebrate blood comes from hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that contains iron atoms. Hemoglobin’s job is to deliver oxygen—and its iron atoms, which grab onto oxygen, make our blood look red. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. pages.description: Paleontologists are resurrecting a famous Egyptian fossil site after a World War II air raid obliterated its most spectacular dinosaur discoveries—and their findings reveal a world even deadlier than expected.

Enter your email here . To Egyptologists, the Bahariya Oasis is known as the Valley of Golden Mummies, a necropolis where archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of gilded and decorated mummies dating back to the Greco-Roman era, roughly 2,000 years ago. But to paleontologists, the oasis is sacred because of something far older and far more legendary: Spinosaurus . The first ever specimen of this ferocious river monster was collected here more than a hundred years ago, along with fossils of several other enigmatic dinosaurs. Until they were lost forever, casualties of the World War II bombing that destroyed much of Munich. Swallowed by the flames, these dinosaurs essentially went extinct twice. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. There may be no better illustration of the critical and integral role the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has played in the history of our nation’s health than the timely juxtaposition of two anniversaries occurring this year – our nation’s 250th and the FDA’s 120th. That’s because this confluence underscores how, for nearly half of our nation’s existence, Americans have relied on, and benefited from, the FDA’s oversight of our food, medical products, veterinary products, cosmetics, and so much more. The FDA’s regulatory role began in 1906 with the passage of the Pure Food and Drugs Act, which authorized the Bureau of Chemistry—the FDA’s immediate predecessor—to regulate contaminated, misbranded, and dangerous foods and medicines. The agency did not receive its present name, the Food and Drug Administration, until 1930. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. Proposed funding is divided among 12 subcommittees, which hold hearings. Each handles funding for different government functions such as defense spending or energy and water. Wealthy and powerful, it had just defeated the Etruscan city of Veii, amassed an immense war chest, and doubled its territory. But then, out of the blue, the republic suffered the unthinkable: occupation by a Celtic people, the Gauls. This was the first time that Rome and Gaul would face off, but it would not be the last. Over the coming centuries, the Romans and the Gauls would clash many times. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Jurassic Shield By Riley Black Published June 26, 2015 • 7 min read Some dinosaurs are better at hiding than others. There’s no single reason for their edge. Some were rare. Others too small to gain much notice from the paleontologists who were set on finding large, imposing specimens for museum centerpieces. Still more became preserved in slices of rock that haven’t gained the attention of the most famed quarries. Whatever the reasons, though, a big, heavily-armored dinosaur was able to escape the notice of paleontologists despite over a century of Jurassic exploration. North America’s Morrison Formation is a fossiliferous wonderland. Spectacular bonebeds dot its reach from Canada to Mexico, and it was one of the focal points for the great Bone Wars between O.C. Marsh and E.D. Cope in the late 19th century. Apatosaurus , Allosaurus , Camarasaurus , Diplodocus and more were the products of that feud. Strangest of all was Stegosaurus – a 30-foot-long quadruped with a tiny head, flashy plates along its back, and a set of four spikes jutting from the tip of its tail. Marsh named the bizarre animal in 1877, and ever since Stegosaurus has held the banner for the plated, spiky armored dinosaurs that were eventually replaced by ankylosaurs. pages.text: The Last Stationery Shop in France Keeping a 400-Year-Old Tradition Alive | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE The Last Stationery Shop in France Keeping a 400-Year-Old Tradition Alive Once used for presidents, diplomats, and luxury stationers, the centuries-old art of pendulum stamping dwindled to a single master printer before finding new life in Paris. Manual pendulum stamping was once popular in the 19th century. A decreased demand a result of the digital age has led the craft to nearly disappear. Yann Garin By Lauren Paige Richeson Published October 15, 2026 Long before our messages arrived with a buzz, a letter could introduce itself by touch. Without even glimpsing the handwriting inside, the paper itself announced a family name, a profession, a crest, or a ceremony—not merely a decoration, but a declaration. In Paris, one of the most refined ways to create that impression was with timbrage au balancier , or pendulum stamping. Developed in the 19th-century world of engraving and correspondence, the technique gave calling cards, invitations, letterheads, and envelope flaps something ordinary ink could not provide: a feeling. Everything from a coat of arms to a pair of initials could rise from the page in dense color and varying depths. But as correspondence slipped from paper to pixels and luxury printing pressed faster towards mechanized processes, the manual craft began to lose the world that sustained it. By 2022, the art rested in one last pair of hands: Éric Lejeusne, France’s last manual pendulum stamper, who was preparing to retire after decades in the trade

How did people survive? | National Geographic During the Little Ice Age, the Northern Hemisphere experienced long stretches of temperatures so cold that crops failed and rivers froze—like the Scheldt River, depicted here outside of Antwerp, Belgium, in a 1593 oil painting by Lucas van Valckenborch. Photograph by incamerastock, Alamy Stock Photo Premium ENVIRONMENT The Little Ice Age was brutal. How did people survive? From roughly the 16th to 19th centuries, much of the Earth was gripped by a persistent frigid cold. It left ripples through history—and some lessons for today’s climate crisis. By Kieran Mulvaney Published February 20, 2024 Thousands of people walking and playing across the frozen River Thames. Soldiers on horseback capturing ships stuck in the ice. Indigenous populations using snowshoes to outfox English interlopers. Accused witches put on trial as their communities struggled to explain crop failures and extreme cold. These were some of the images that define the Little Ice Age—a period of several centuries last millennium in which parts of the Northern Hemisphere grappled with a persistent cold. But what caused the Little Ice Age, how long did it last, how did people adapt to its frigid grip—and what lessons can we learn as we enter our own period of climatic change? ( Broken Baculum a Sign of Painful Ice Age Injury) What is the Little Ice Age—and what caused it? The Little Ice Age was not a true ice age—average cooling was probably only in the order of 0.5 degrees Celsius , or 1 degree Fahrenheit—nor was it consistently cold.

People gather around the Mona Lisa painting in Paris, three years after it was stolen from the Louvre by Vincenzo Peruggia in 1911. The theft is one of the most famous in the museum's history. Roger-Viollet, Getty Images By Erin Blakemore Published October 19, 2025 It took just seven minutes for a group of audacious thieves to pull off what may have been one of the most daring crimes in modern art: the theft of Napoleonic-era jewels from the Louvre in Paris on the morning of October 19. The heist, which took place while the museum was open to the public, involved a variety of jewels once owned by members of the French monarchy, including an emerald necklace and earrings that Napoleon gave his second wife Marie-Louise for their wedding. Now, questions are raging about how masked men could successfully evade security and nab priceless objets d’art from one of the most important art institutions in the world. It’s far from the first time. The museum has a longstanding history of shocking break-ins and unsolved thefts—despite being built precisely to protect the nation’s cultural heritage in the wake of a bloody revolution. The opening ceremony won’t take place in a stadium but—bucking tradition—outside on the River Seine. For the Parade of Nations, boats carrying the participating teams will glide by an estimated 300,000 spectators congregated on the quays. Bathed in myth and memory, the Seine is the lifeblood of the city that sprang up on its banks. Along this “main street,” as Napoleon called it, photogenic Pari­sian landmarks are on proud display, oozing grandeur and majesty. It’s so cen­tral to the city’s existence that building numbers are linked to the river: Those on perpendicular streets begin their num­bering closest to the Seine, while on parallel streets building numbers ascend in the direction of the current. “For Parisians, there’s a strong historical and visceral attachment to the river,” says Pierre Rabadan, the deputy mayor in charge of sport, the Olympic and Paralympic Games, and the Seine. ( Paris made an Olympic-size effort to clean up the Seine—did they succeed? ) The genesis of Paris From its source in Burgundy, the Seine flows 483 miles to reach the sea at Le Havre, with the capital sitting nearly in the middle. pages.text: The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes Climate change is exposing once-submerged churches, castles and petroglyphs—and threatening their survival. The Basilica of Saint Neophytos, the likely site of early Christianity's Nicene Council, used to be submerged beneath Lake İznik. But drought has caused the lake's waters to recede, exposing the ancient structure. Sercan Ozkurnazl, Getty Images By Katie Nadworny Published September 24, 2026 Mustafa Şahin used to spend much more of his time below water. As the founder of Turkey’s first underwater archaeology department, he practiced his work in the country’s lakes, diving deep to uncover important historical ruins. In 2014, he found the Basilica of Saint Neophytos—a contender for the home of the original Nicene Council —in Lake İznik, a discovery that Archaeology Magazine and The Archaeological Institute of America deemed one of the most important that year. But Mustafa isn’t diving anymore. His work as head archaeologist of the basilica now keeps him out of the lake, because Saint Neophytos is no longer under İznik’s waters. It sits on dry ground. Lake İznik is facing a crisis and it isn’t alone. Turkey is losing most of its lakes at an alarming rate: close to 75 percent are in the process of disappearing, many within the last decade. pages.text: The world's glaciers are melting faster than we thought, new research shows | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT The world's glaciers are melting faster than we thought, new research shows Glaciers have survived through a delicate balance of gain and loss. A new study shows just how much the scale has tipped. Drone light dramatically illuminates the Pastoruri Glacier in Cordillera Blanca, Peru. Glaciers like these provide drinking water to communities during their dry seasons. As they melt, this water supply dwindles and lost ice causes seas to rise. Photograph by Reuben Wu, Nat Geo Image Collection By Theo Nicitopoulos Published November 15, 2024 In 1971, researchers made a surprising discovery while studying Greenland's ice: Temperatures over the island spiked by very large amounts within short periods thousands of years ago. The finding showed that abrupt warming could happen over just several decades and changed how they thought about natural climate change. ( Arctic Ice Isn't Doomed Yet—Here's How to Save It) Today, the world is the in the grips of another major shift, this time due to anthropogenic activities. And scientists are making predictions about how ice will soon evolve as temperatures warm. In a new study published today in the journal The Cryosphere , researchers modeled how much glaciers will melt by the year 2100. The results show that more ice will disappear than what's predicted in the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report, generally considered the scientific consensus on the state of climate change. pages.text: The ‘Blessed Lizard’ That Inherited the Earth After Its Worst Apocalypse | National Geographic SCIENCE The ‘Blessed Lizard’ That Inherited the Earth After Its Worst Apocalypse Shakajlura riojanensis , a newly discovered Triassic apex predator, ruled the land millions of years before the rise of giant dinosaurs. Emerging from the ashes of the planet’s worst mass extinction, Shakajlura riojanensis was an ancient crocodile cousin that reigned over the Triassic before large dinosaurs appeared. By Joshua Rapp Learn Published August 12, 2026 Paleontologists in Argentina have discovered a deadly prehistoric crocodile with “blade-like serrated” teeth that triumphed over the Triassic some 237 million years ago, before large dinosaurs arrived and usurped the throne. “We consider these as the apex predators of the Triassic,” says Ariel Cardillo, a doctoral candidate in vertebrate paleontology at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET) and lead author of the study. “They were really large animals compared to the rest of the ecosystem.” From snarling snout to tail, the new species Shakajlura riojanensis would have been nearly 20 feet long. “This may not look like much, but in the Triassic, most of the fauna is pretty small,” Cardillo says. Shakajlura ’s bite was likely as powerful as modern-day crocs, and every tooth was “like a knife pointing out of the mouth,” he adds. Representations of dogs, often in the form of gargoyles, can be spotted in Christian monuments across Europe. They symbolized various admirable qualities, including loyalty, domestic comfort, and protection. IVAN VDOVIN/ALAMY/CORDON PRESS By Monica Walker Vadillo Published October 24, 2025 In the second or third century A.D., an anonymous author in Alexandria, Egypt, composed a text entitled Physiologus, or The Naturalist. The work was soon widely copied and comprised of 48 or 49 chapters. Each was dedicated to a specific animal and included an illustration, a description of its characteristics, and a story—part natural observation, part imaginative anecdote—about its behavior. One such story, for example, features the lion. It was said that lion cubs were born lifeless and watched over by their mother until the father, king of the beasts, arrived and breathed life into them. By Michael Greshko Published January 1, 2020 • 7 min read Sixty-six million years ago, the ground of western North America trembled with the footfalls of a tyrant: Tyrannosaurus rex . But despite a wealth of T. rex remains pulled from the region’s Cretaceous-period rocks, scientists have had few clues about how the celebrity dinosaur grew from a hatchling to a gargantuan predator—until now. In a study published in Science Advances on Wednesday , researchers reveal a stunningly detailed analysis on cross-sections of bone from juvenile tyrannosaurs. An illustration shows what Duonychus tsogtbaatari might have looked like. Unlike its therizinosaur brethren, the new species had only two claws instead of three. Illustration by Masato Hattori By Riley Black Published March 25, 2025 Therizinosaurs were some of the strangest dinosaurs of all time. Descended from carnivores , the prehistoric reptiles were plant-eaters and had fuzzy feathered bodies, small heads with peg-like teeth in their jaws, bulbous stomachs that acted like fermenting vats for heaps of vegetation, and impressively large claws on each of their hands. Their build and claws have drawn comparisons to sloths, but some of these reptiles stood over 13 feet tall and weighed more than five tons. Now paleontologists have uncovered a therizinosaur that stands out even among its unusual relatives—because it’s missing a finger. Described in the journal iScience today, the new dinosaur comes from rocks in Mongolia’s Gobi Desert that are over 90 million years old. Back in 2012, paleontologists from the Mongolian Academy of Sciences initially unearthed parts of the spine, ribs, hips, and shoulders, and finally found two complete hands. Illustration by Henry Sharpe By Asher Elbein Published October 7, 2026 Ever since the first well-preserved mosasaur skeletons were found in the late 1800s, paleontologists have recognized that these flippered sea lizards lived in the ocean. But in the 2010s, a reassessment of mosasaur anatomy suggested they had relatively stiff bodies, and one study showed that their tails ended in a shark-like tail fin. pages.title: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat
pages.description: An intense selection process and long preparation helped set the crew up for cohabitation in a 3D-printed replication of the Red Planet's environment in Houston. There, they practiced Marswalks, disrupted communications with people on Earth and food cultivation
pages.text: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat Skip to main content Four individuals participated in NASA's second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

pages.text: This Mysterious Combination Lock Sank in a 1583 Shipwreck. When Engineers Cracked the Code, It Clicked Open for the First Time in More Than 400 Years Skip to main content The lock features four rotating dials, and each dial has six letters. Museum Wales In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle. Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. When they tested it out, the lock clicked open for the first time in more than four centuries. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant,” Hughes tells BBC Wales ’ Meleri Williams. “I’m delighted—truly thrilled.” The Ann Francis was traveling from Spain to England when a storm swept in on December 28, 1583. The winds blew it off course, and it ultimately wrecked off Margam Beach in southern Wales. According to a parish register, 14 sailors died in December 1583, and these men may have been the Ann Francis ’ crew. pages.title: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic
pages.description: Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question.
pages.text: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic SCIENCE This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question. Unearthed in a rare Saharan fossil site in Niger, Spinosaurus mirabilis had a large head crest that may have signaled a message to rivals competing for resources or territory along the way. artwork by Dani Navarro By Helen Thompson Published February 19, 2026 Under the central Saharan sun, paleontologist Daniel Vidal spotted a mysterious bone poking out of the ground during an excavation in Niger. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. Now, the researchers report the crest belonged to an entirely new species— Spinosaurus mirabilis —that roamed the area’s ancient river ecosystem some 95 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous. They published their discovery Thursday in Science . The new species adds to a heated debate over how these puzzling (and popular) dinosaurs lived and hunted in water.

The harbour wall of Lyme Regis is also known as The Cobb. Thomas Faull, Getty Images By Jessica Prupas Published August 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. It’s a badge locals wear proudly: you’ll find a weather-beaten statue of celebrated fossil hunter Mary Anning overlooking Church Cliff Beach. In 1823, while wandering Lyme Regis’s coastline, she unearthed the world’s first complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus and, nearly two centuries after her death, the town remains a magnet for excavators. Lyme Regis' seafront is a walkable promenade best discovered at dusk. Graham Custance, Getty Images Where should I begin? The main strip is Front Beach, which fringes the promenade with its wash of pastel huts. On its western end, you’ll find Shoreline Sauna , whose wood-fired, Nordic-style saunas sit right on the sand. Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues. The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life. Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field. The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland. Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that. "I've been training quite a bit. More than 30 years later, the collective, led by Big Tony Fisher, still fills sold-out venues with heavyweight percussion and call-and-response lyrics. TSCA Section 21 Under TSCA section 21, any person may petition EPA to initiate a proceeding for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule or order under: Section 4 -- rules or orders requiring chemical testing; Section 6 -- rules imposing regulatory controls on chemicals; Section 8 -- rules requiring information; or Section 5(e) or (f) -- orders affecting new chemical substances. The petition must be filed in EPA's Office of the Administrator and set forth the facts that are claimed to establish the necessity for the action requested. EPA is required to grant or deny the petition within 90 days from the day the petition is filed with EPA. If EPA grants the petition, EPA must promptly commence an appropriate proceeding. If EPA denies the petition, the reasons for denial must be published in the Federal Register.
